paragraph.text: "person" is a concept we created, and that we already apply to companies, ships and rivers. Using it to decide who may be killed is choosing the definition that produces the desired conclusion. By the classic criterion of personhood, Locke's, human babies aren't persons either, and some animals come closer to the criterion than they do.
"Animals aren't people. People are people, animals are animals."
Only persons have full moral status and can hold rights.
A person is a self-aware being, able to recognize itself as the same over time, to make plans and take on responsibilities.
Animals aren't persons in this sense.
So animals don't have full moral status and may be used.

P2's definition comes from John Locke, who described a person as a thinking, intelligent being, with reason and reflection, able to consider itself as the same thinking thing in different times and places. It's a
definition, not a biological one: it doesn't say "member of the human species".
, used in courts: a person is whoever can hold rights and duties. This was the criterion adopted by the majority of the New York Court of Appeals in the case of Happy the elephant, in 2022.
fails because P2 and P3 can't both be true without excluding human babies, and because P1 makes a definition we chose into the source of moral value.
"Are you comparing a pig to a person?"
"It isn't a subject of anything; it's property."
"So will the chicken get a passport?"
"A person is a self-aware being, able to recognize itself over time and take on responsibilities."
"Legal personhood presupposes the capacity to bear duties."
"Everything in its place: people are people, animals are animals."

Words are invented by us. "Person" is one of them. Did you know that, in the law, a company is also a "person"? It has no body and feels nothing, and still it can have rights on paper. So calling someone a person isn't what decides whether they can feel pain. What decides it is having a body and a mind that feel. A pig has those.

This argument settles the question by the choice of word. If "person" means self-awareness and plans for the future, then newborn babies aren't persons either, and elephants, great apes and dolphins come closer to the criterion than they do. If "person" means a legal holder of rights, remember that companies are legal persons and that the Whanganui River, in New Zealand, was granted legal personhood in 2017. Personhood is a tool we grant, not a fact of nature.
"Does a company feel pain? Then why is it a person and the pig isn't?"
The word "person" is used in at least three senses, and the argument switches between them as convenient.
All humans, no animals. But then "person" is just another name for species, and the argument becomes A10

This is the book's clearest case of the

text.bold: 1. In the psychological sense, it proves too much.

paragraph.text: By Locke's criterion, a three-month-old baby isn't a person: they don't recognize themselves as the same being over time or make plans. Whoever holds P2 must accept that killing a baby wouldn't harm a person, or abandon the criterion.

text.bold: 2. In the psychological sense, it includes animals.

paragraph.text: Elephants recognize their own image in a mirror (Plotnik, de Waal and Reiss, 2006). Scrub jays (

) remember what they hid, where and how long ago, adjusting their behavior to the type of food, which has been called episodic-like memory (Clayton and Dickinson, 1998). If that's the criterion, it doesn't divide species the way the argument wants.

text.bold: 3. In the legal sense, personhood is a tool, not a fact.

paragraph.text: Companies are legal persons and feel nothing. In 2017, New Zealand recognized the Whanganui River as a legal person, with legal representatives, through the Te Awa Tupua Act. In 2022, Ecuador's Constitutional Court recognized individual animals as subjects of rights (see A7). The law grants personhood when it decides to protect something; the question is whether there's reason to protect, not whether the label has already been granted.

text.bold: 4. The Happy case shows the argument in action, and its fragility.

paragraph.text: In 2022, the New York Court of Appeals denied, by 5 votes to 2, the habeas corpus sought for Happy the elephant, holding that the writ applies only to human beings and that a person is someone who can bear duties and social responsibilities. In dissent, Judge Rivera observed that humans without full rights have been able to use habeas corpus, and that the majority failed to explain why an autonomous being of another species couldn't; Judge Wilson recalled that the writ was historically extended to enslaved people, who also had no recognized duties.

text.bold: 5. The moral question doesn't depend on the word.

paragraph.text: Even if we agree to call only humans persons, there's still a being who feels pain, fear and pleasure. Sentientism doesn't need the concept of person: it only needs someone for whom things can go well or badly.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: person as a moral concept, not a label

The serious reply says "person" isn't an arbitrary label: it marks the kind of being whose life has special value, because it has projects, projects itself into the future and can lose more than pleasure by dying. Stronger protection falls on these beings, which would explain why killing a human is worse than killing a fish. Philosophically, this appears in Jeff McMahan's time-relative interest account.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
Even if killing a person is worse than killing an animal, it doesn't follow that killing an animal is permitted, still less for the pleasure of a meal.

The concept of person isn't philosophical rubbish. It captures something real: beings with self-awareness, memory of themselves and plans for the future may lose more by dying, and can be harmed in ways other beings can't, such as by humiliation or broken promises. Legal personhood is also a complex instrument, involving representation, procedures and responsibilities, and extending it requires careful institutional design, not just good intentions.

The mistake is turning this concept into the gateway to moral consideration. None of it answers the question that matters: is there someone there for whom what we do is good or bad? If there is, calling that someone a person or not is a decision about vocabulary, not about what we owe them.
